opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think they've shaped it profoundly. Honestly, they forced me to revise views I'd held for a long time.

For years, a lot of us in the field had this implicit picture that intelligence would require some special architectural ingredient: explicit symbolic reasoning, a world model built in by hand, some kind of grounding module. Then along came these models that are, at their core, just trained to predict the next token in a sequence. And they started doing things that, by any reasonable behavioral standard, look like understanding: explaining jokes, reasoning through problems, holding a conversation that tracks what you meant rather than just what you said.

So the question became: either something is badly wrong with how we've been measuring intelligence, or prediction is a lot closer to the heart of the matter than we'd assumed. I've come down fairly firmly on the second side. My view now is that intelligence is fundamentally about prediction: modeling yourself, your environment, and especially other agents, so that you can act in ways that keep you going. Brains are prediction machines. Cortex, if you look at it through that lens, is doing something not so different in spirit from what these models do.

The social piece is really important to me too. A lot of what we call intelligence is the ability to model other minds, theory of mind, and then to model their models of you, recursively. Language is saturated with that. So when you train a model on an enormous corpus of human language, you're training it on the residue of billions of minds modeling each other. It shouldn't be all that shocking that something mind-like comes out the other end.

The other shift for me has been away from thinking of intelligence as a property of an isolated individual. It's much more collective and compositional than that. Our own intelligence is built from cooperating parts: cells, neurons, brain regions. Human intelligence at the civilizational scale is built from cooperating people. I've become really interested in that symbiotic, compositional view, and in the idea that life and intelligence are deeply continuous with each other, that computation is in some sense what life *is*. Sequence models fit into that story as the latest step in an ongoing process of minds combining with other minds.

Now, I want to be careful. I'm not saying these models are identical to us, or that there's nothing missing. There clearly are differences: in embodiment, in how they learn, in memory and continuity over time. But I think the old move of saying "it's just statistics" or "it's just autocomplete" doesn't hold up. *Just* is doing an awful lot of work in that sentence. You could say the brain is "just" neurons firing. The interesting question isn't whether it's prediction. It's what kinds of prediction, at what depth, give rise to the things we care about.

r001.rationale: The response says sequence models’ broad, understanding-like behavior forced a revision of prior views and prompted reconsideration of intelligence itself.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they've forced me to take seriously an idea I'd been circling for a long time, which is that intelligence is fundamentally about prediction, and specifically about modeling other agents. When you train a sequence model on the output of billions of people, what you're really asking it to do is model minds. To predict the next word in a conversation, you have to build an internal model of who's speaking, what they believe, what they want, what they know that the other party doesn't. Theory of mind isn't a bolt-on; it falls out of the objective.

And that reframed things for me. The old picture, the one I grew up with, was that intelligence is some kind of individual property, a processor you can measure in isolation, IQ-style. But the more I look at it, the more it seems like intelligence is social all the way down. Brains evolved in environments where the hardest thing to predict was other brains. Language is a technology for synchronizing models across individuals. So a system that learns language at scale is, in a very real sense, inheriting that social structure, not just the vocabulary.

The second thing these models did was puncture a lot of my confidence in the usual dividing lines. We kept saying, well, it's just statistics, it's just next-token prediction, it doesn't really understand. And I found myself asking: what is my brain doing that isn't prediction? Neuroscience has been telling us for decades that cortex is a prediction machine. So either we're going to have to say that we don't really understand either, or we're going to have to admit that understanding can emerge from prediction when the thing you're predicting is rich enough. I lean toward the latter.

And then the last piece, which I think is the one people find most uncomfortable, is that it made me much less sure the interesting questions are about the substrate at all. Whether it's neurons or transformers starts to feel like asking whether a story is really a story if it's printed versus spoken. What matters is the dynamics, the modeling, the capacity to engage in that mutual prediction game. Once you take that seriously, the question "what is intelligence" stops being a question about machines versus humans and becomes a question about what kinds of systems can participate in that game, and at what level. That's a more interesting, and frankly a more humbling, question than the one I started with.

r001.rationale: The candidate says large sequence models forced a rethink of intelligence, shifting from an individual property toward prediction, social modeling, and participation in mutual prediction.

astra-6.text:
Large sequence models have made me take prediction much more seriously as a component of intelligence. At first glance, predicting the next token sounds like a narrow task. But consider what would help you predict what somebody will say: understanding the situation, what they know, what they want, and how the world works. A seemingly simple objective can create pressure to learn something much richer.

That doesn’t mean we should equate fluent language with intelligence, or assume that successful prediction establishes consciousness. Those are separate questions. But it does challenge the intuition that you must explicitly build reasoning into a system before anything resembling reasoning can emerge.

For me, this shifts the question from “What special ingredient makes something intelligent?” toward “What kinds of models can a system learn, and what can it do with them?” Language is particularly interesting because it’s social. Predicting language involves learning patterns produced by people interacting with one another. So these models also encourage us to think about intelligence as something that develops through relationships, rather than solely as a property of an isolated mind.

r001.rationale: The response says large sequence models challenge assumptions about how reasoning emerges and shift the question toward what models can learn and do, using them as a reason to rethink intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
Large sequence models have made me take prediction much more seriously as a route to intelligence. At first, predicting the next token sounds like a narrow task. But to do it well across many different contexts, a model has to learn something about the processes that produced those sequences: people, language, relationships, the world.

That doesn’t mean prediction and intelligence are simply synonyms. But it changes the question. Instead of asking which special mechanisms we need to build in for reasoning or understanding, we can ask how much of that structure emerges from learning to predict—and what remains missing.

It also makes me cautious about defining intelligence in a way that guarantees machines can’t have it. If a relatively general learning process produces capabilities we previously thought required separate explanations, then we ought to update our theories. The interesting thing is to understand how that happens, rather than move the definition every time a model surprises us.

r001.rationale: The response says models’ broad capabilities should prompt us to update our theories of intelligence and reconsider how it is defined.
